title: Three Ways to Span a Gap

shot.narration: Here is a gap of twenty-four metres, with a bank on each side. A bridge has to carry a deck from one bank to the other.
shot.visual_purpose: Show the empty site and the span to be crossed [SITE_HOLD 1/1: the empty shared site: the gap any of the structures must span]

shots.explanation: the empty shared site: the gap any of the structures must span

shot.narration: The simplest answer is a beam. In this timber bridge, beams run from one support to the next, and the deck rests on top of them.
shot.visual_purpose: Introduce the timber beam bridge and its spanning members [ASSEMBLE_IN 1/2: timber_beam_bridge assembles into the shown empty site (its parts drop in by assembly layer)]

shots.explanation: timber_beam_bridge assembles into the shown empty site (its parts drop in by assembly layer)

shot.narration: A stone arch works differently. It is built from wedge-shaped stones called voussoirs, with a keystone at the top of each arch.
shot.visual_purpose: Introduce the masonry arch and show one arch ring's voussoirs and keystone [CLOSEUP_HIGHLIGHT 1/2: establish stone_arch_bridge with arch_ring glowing]

shot.narration: A truss takes another approach: many straight members joined into triangles.
shot.visual_purpose: Introduce the truss and its triangulated members [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold steel_truss_bridge, glowing truss_web]

shot.narration: The triangles can be arranged in different patterns. A Pratt truss has vertical members and diagonals that slope down towards the centre. A Warren truss uses alternating diagonals, with no verticals.
shot.visual_purpose: Compare the Pratt and Warren web patterns on the same chords [HIGHLIGHT_REPLACE_HIGHLIGHT 1/3: glow the parts of steel_truss_bridge that will change]
